opus-5.5.text:
Sure. Let me first recall the setup. In our work we use synthetic data generated by a probabilistic context-free grammar. We call it the random hierarchy model. You have a tree: a high-level symbol at the top generates a few lower-level symbols, those generate others, and so on down to the visible tokens. A key ingredient is that each symbol can be produced by many different "synonymous" combinations of lower-level symbols. Learning an abstraction means learning that these different low-level patterns are equivalent, so you can collapse them into a single latent variable.

So how does a network discover that two sequences of tokens are synonyms? In next-token prediction, the only signal it has is statistical. Two synonymous groups of tokens have the same correlations with the rest of the sequence, in particular with the token you're trying to predict. If the network can measure those correlations, it can group the patterns together. The difficulty is that these correlations are weak, and they get weaker the further up the tree you go. A token is linked to a distant part of the context only through a chain of intermediate latent variables. At each level, the randomness of which synonym was chosen dilutes the signal. So the correlation decays rapidly with the depth of the common ancestor. To resolve a small correlation above the sampling noise, you need many examples. That's why we find that the number of samples needed to learn each new level grows like a power law, with an effective context window that grows with the training set size.

Now consider what happens if, instead of predicting the raw next token, you predict a nearby concept that has already been learned, meaning a latent variable at some intermediate level. You've removed a whole layer of noise. You no longer have to go through the many-to-one mapping from latent to tokens on the output side. The variability coming from which synonym was chosen at the lower levels has already been factored out. Neighboring latent variables are much more strongly correlated with each other than raw tokens far apart are. So the signal-to-noise ratio you need to detect the next level of structure is much better. As a result, the sample complexity to climb one more step in the hierarchy is reduced.

You can think of it as a bootstrapping argument. Once you've built a representation at level ℓ, doing prediction in that representation space makes level ℓ+1 look "local" and "shallow" again. You're effectively solving the easy first-level problem repeatedly, instead of one very hard deep problem. With raw next-token prediction, you're always paying the cost of the full chain of dilution between the observed tokens and the abstraction you want to learn.

I think this connects to the intuition behind approaches like JEPA, or predicting in latent space more generally. The point isn't that next-token prediction can't learn abstractions. It can, and our theory explains how. The point is that it's data-inefficient, because it insists on reconstructing details that are irrelevant to the abstraction. Predicting at the level of concepts discards that irrelevant variability. In these hierarchical models, that's precisely where the savings in data come from.

r001.rationale: It says correlations weaken with distance up the tree and decay rapidly with the depth of the common ancestor.

r002.rationale: It describes sample needs growing like a power law across hierarchy levels, but does not state that data requirements are exponential in tree depth.

r003.rationale: It does not connect an exponential dependence on tree depth to polynomial dependence on input dimensionality.

r004.rationale: It explains that predicting a nearby learned latent concept removes output-side noise and provides stronger correlations than predicting raw, distant tokens.

r005.rationale: It says weak correlations require many examples to distinguish from sampling noise, while stronger latent correlations improve signal-to-noise and reduce sample complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So the setup here is a generative model of data that has a hierarchical, tree-like structure. You can think of it like a context-free grammar: at the top there is a class label, or a root symbol, and it generates a few high-level features, each of which generates lower-level features, and so on, down to the leaves, which are the actual tokens you observe, pixels or words. The key point is that the latent variables at intermediate levels of the tree are hidden. The learner never sees them directly; it only sees the leaves.

Now, when you train with next-token prediction, what the model is actually doing, in our analysis, is learning correlations between a token and its context. And the way it discovers an abstraction, say a latent variable one level up in the tree, is by noticing that certain groups of tokens are statistically interchangeable: they predict the same thing about the rest of the sequence. To detect that, you have to measure correlations between leaves, and those correlations are weak, because they are mediated by several layers of randomness in the generative process. So you need many samples just to see the signal above the noise. And the deeper the abstraction, the farther apart the relevant tokens are in the tree, and the weaker the correlation, which is why the sample complexity grows very fast with depth, essentially like a power of the vocabulary size at each level you climb.

The alternative we considered is: suppose you have already learned the concepts at level one, meaning you can replace groups of tokens by the latent symbol they correspond to. Now, instead of predicting the next raw token, you predict the next latent symbol from neighboring latent symbols. The correlations you need to measure are now between variables that are one step apart in the tree, rather than many steps apart. So the signal is strong, you need far fewer samples, and the number you need is roughly independent of how deep you are, because at each stage you are only ever solving a local problem. You effectively collapse the tree one layer at a time, and each layer costs you about the same.

So the gap is really about what quantity you are trying to estimate. Next-token prediction forces you to resolve long-range, weak correlations through the whole hierarchy at once. Predicting nearby learned concepts turns that into a sequence of short-range, strong-correlation problems. Statistically, that is just a much cheaper thing to learn, and it is why we think a curriculum, or a model that builds representations bottom-up, can be dramatically more data-efficient than a flat predictor on raw tokens.

r001.rationale: It says correlations are weak when mediated through several tree layers and weaker for abstractions farther apart in the tree.

r002.rationale: It says sample complexity grows with depth like a power of the vocabulary size at each level, communicating exponential growth across levels.

r003.rationale: It does not relate the depth dependence to polynomial dependence on input dimensionality.

r004.rationale: It explains that predicting neighboring learned latent symbols uses stronger, local correlations than predicting raw tokens across the hierarchy.

r005.rationale: It states that weak correlations require many samples to rise above noise, while strong correlations require far fewer.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that predicting a nearby concept gives you a more direct signal about the abstraction that the two concepts share. Think of a tree: two nearby leaves have a common ancestor relatively low in the tree. If you learn to predict one from the other, that common ancestor is useful, and many different pairs can provide evidence for it. So you can pool information across examples rather than learn each pair separately.

Next-token prediction asks for something more specific. You have to predict the particular token, including details that may not be determined by the shared abstraction. The signal about that abstraction is therefore mixed with variation at the leaves. In these tree-like models, this can mean you need many more observations before you can reliably extract it.

So the distinction is not that next-token prediction cannot learn abstractions. It is that the prediction target changes how directly the training signal exposes them. Predicting related concepts can make the shared structure much easier to learn.

r001.rationale: It contrasts nearby concepts with variation at the leaves, but does not state that concept correlations decrease with tree distance.

r002.rationale: It says next-token prediction may require many more observations, but does not state an exponential dependence on tree depth.

r003.rationale: It does not connect data requirements to polynomial dependence on input dimensionality.

r004.rationale: It explains that predicting a nearby concept gives a more direct signal about a shared abstraction, while next-token prediction includes leaf-level details not determined by that abstraction.

r005.rationale: It says examples can be pooled and the shared structure is easier to learn, but does not explain that stronger correlations require fewer samples to measure reliably.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that predicting a nearby concept gives you a much more direct signal about the abstraction they share. Imagine that concepts are the leaves of a tree, and the internal nodes represent increasingly general categories. Two nearby leaves have a recent common ancestor. So, even though the particular examples vary, their relationship repeatedly gives you information about that ancestor.

Next-token prediction gives you a less direct signal. You have to predict a particular token, and that depends on many details beyond the shared abstraction. You can improve prediction by learning those details without necessarily discovering the higher-level structure. The evidence for that structure is therefore spread across many different observations.

So the distinction is not that next-token prediction cannot learn abstractions. It can. But in these models, the amount of data you need depends strongly on the task: predicting related concepts concentrates the useful signal, whereas predicting the next token requires more examples to extract it.

r001.rationale: It describes nearby leaves as sharing a recent ancestor, but does not state that correlations decrease as concepts get farther apart in the tree.

r002.rationale: It says next-token prediction requires more examples, but does not state that the amount grows exponentially with tree depth.

r003.rationale: It does not connect an exponential dependence on tree depth to a polynomial dependence on input dimensionality.

r004.rationale: It explains that nearby concepts provide a direct signal about their shared abstraction, while next-token targets depend on details beyond that structure.

r005.rationale: It says nearby concepts concentrate useful signal, but does not explain that stronger correlations take fewer samples to measure reliably.
